title: Why the 'Haves' Come Out Ahead: Speculations on the Limits of Legal Change
author: Marc Galanter

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source does not address AI capability, legal engineering, verification or task-specific evaluation. Instead, it reframes reliable and accessible legal delivery around structural litigation costs, institutional passivity and chronic court overload, arguing that these conditions advantage resource-rich parties and pressure claimants to settle.
qs: In several ways overload creates pressures on claimants to settle rather than to adjudicate:      (a) by causing delay (thereby discounting the value of re-           covery);      (b) by raising costs (of keeping the case alive);      (c) by inducing institutional incumbents to place a high val-           ue on clearing dockets, discouraging full-dress adjudic-

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Galanter does not assess AI’s jagged capabilities, verification needs or selective deployment. He instead reframes effective legal change around structural inequalities in party organization, legal services and institutional implementation. This reinforces the cluster’s access-to-remedy caution, but redirects its technology-centred proposition toward building long-term strategic capacity for disadvantaged parties.
qs: Our analysis suggests that breaking the interlocked advant-  ages of the "haves" requires attention not only to the level of rules, but also to institutional facilities, legal services and organ- ization of parties.
Similarly, even OSs who have procured favorable judgments may     experience difficulty at the execution stage.

st.t: Legal specialization: Client relationships fragment expertise
st.an: Galanter accepts that specialization is structured by client type and adversarial side, then materially extends the proposition by showing that specialist expertise only partly offsets repeat-player advantages. He also links episodic client relationships and professional organization to routine service, divided loyalties and unequal strategic capacity.
qs: We may divide specialists into (1)those specialized by field of law (patent, divorce, etc.), (2) those specialized by the kind of party represented (for example, house counsel), and (3)those specialized by both field of law and "side" or party (personal injury plaintiff, criminal defense, lab- or).
But this is short of overcoming the fundamental strategic advantages of RPs-their      capacity to structure the transaction, play the odds, and  influence  rule-development and enforcement policy.

kp.k: Legal architecture can reinforce inequality despite formal neutrality
kp.d: Galanter's 1974 essay offers a historical, theoretical framework rather than claims about AI. Drawing on commonplaces and explicitly unsystematic literature, he advances tentative conjectures about litigation's capacity for redistributive change. His central argument is that advantages in party organization, legal services, institutional facilities and rules interlock, allowing a formally neutral legal system to preserve or augment existing advantages.
qs: The speculative and tentative nature of the assertions here will be apparent and is acknowledged here wholesale to spare myself and the reader repeated disclaimers.
It points to layers of advantages enjoyed by different (but largely overlapping) classes of "haves"

kp.k: Repeat-player advantage depends on resources and strategic horizons
kp.d: Galanter distinguishes occasional court users, or one-shotters, from repeat players engaged in similar litigation over time. These are ends of a continuum, not identical categories to poor and rich. His ideal repeat player anticipates further litigation, faces relatively low stakes in any individual case and possesses resources to pursue long-term interests. Repeated exposure alone is insufficient: he identifies impoverished recurrent criminal defendants as lacking most repeat-player advantages.
qs: a unit which has had and anticipates repeated litiga- tion, which has low stakes in the outcome of any one case, and which has the resources to pursue its long-run interests.
It is not suggested that RPs are to be equated with "haves" (in terms of power, wealth and status) or OSs with "have-nots."

kp.k: Repeated participation enables prevention, specialization and bargaining credibility
kp.d: The proposed mechanisms include advance intelligence, transaction design, record creation, specialist access, economies of scale, institutional relationships and an established bargaining reputation. Repeat players can spread risks across cases, whereas one-shotters confronting potentially devastating losses may prioritize avoiding their worst outcome. Galanter acknowledges exceptions, including one-shotters whose willingness to exhaust resources or appear irrational can strengthen bargaining threats.
qs: It is the RP who writes the form contract, requires the security deposit, and the like.
They enjoy economies of scale and have low start- up costs for any case.
The RP must establish and maintain credibility as a com- batant.

kp.k: Selective litigation can shape precedents toward repeat players
kp.d: Galanter conjectures that repeat players can sacrifice an immediate monetary result for favorable rules across future cases, settle disputes threatening adverse precedent and litigate promising ones. He supports this mechanism with Macaulay's automobile manufacturer–dealer research, including manufacturers' capacity to spend $40,000 in attorney time on a case settleable for $10,000. He does not treat party strategy as the sole or principal determinant of doctrine: intellectual traditions, judicial preferences and organizational personnel incentives also matter.
qs: RPs can play for rules as well as immediate gains.
Since they expect to litigate again, RPs can select to adjudicate (or appeal) those cases which they regard as most likely to produce favorable rules.
they could afford to invest, for example, $40,000 worth of attorneys' time in a case they could have settled for $10,000.

kp.k: Winning legal rights does not ensure practical enforcement
kp.d: Galanter distinguishes authoritative rule announcements from their effective field-level application, termed penetration. Repeat players can identify consequential rules and finance monitoring and enforcement; one-shotters may lack resources even after winning. As supporting evidence, he reports a 1974 Community Service Society survey of 195 successful individual plaintiffs in two Manhattan Small Claims Courts: only 50% of judgment recipients collected, compared with 82% of settlement recipients.
qs: They can trade off symbolic defeats for tangible gains.
RPs are more likely to be able to invest the matching resources necessary to secure the penetration of rules favorable to them.
only 50% of persons who received judgments were able to collect these through their own efforts or through use of sheriffs and mar- shals.

kp.k: Lawyers improve outcomes without necessarily equalizing clients
kp.d: Galanter reports research associating representation with better outcomes in injury, eviction and criminal cases, but argues that lawyers' own repeat participation does not automatically eliminate client disparities. Repeat clients can purchase sustained, specialized, preventive services, maintain better records and exercise more control over counsel. One-shotter specialists may narrow expertise and bargaining gaps without overcoming the opposing client's capacity to design transactions, spread risks or shape rules.
qs: Parties who have lawyers do better.

Not only would the RP get more tal- ent to begin with, but he would on the whole get greater continu- ity, better record-keeping, more anticipatory or preventive work, more experience and specialized skill in pertinent areas, and more control over counsel.
But this is short of overcoming the fundamental strategic advantages of RPs

kp.k: Professional incentives constrain services for episodic clients
kp.d: Drawing on studies of the contemporary American profession, Galanter describes lawyers serving one-shotters as generally lower in professional status, more often solo practitioners and constrained by client-acquisition restrictions. Small fees and episodic relationships encourage standardized handling; ongoing ties to courts, opposing organizations or referral intermediaries can compete with loyalty to transient clients. Ethics also prevent treating separate clients as one portfolio whose individual cases can be sacrificed for collective gains.
qs: It is not permissible for him to play his series of OSs as if they constituted a single RP.
For the lawyer who services OSs, with his transient clientele, his permanent "client" is the forum, the opposite party, or the intermediary who supplies clients.
But lawyers have a cross-cut- ting interest in preserving complexity and mystique so that client contact with this area of law is rendered problematic.

kp.k: Court passivity and overload amplify resource disparities
kp.d: Courts dependent on party initiative advantage those able to identify claims, pay costs, investigate and present proof. Galanter argues that chronic overload adds delay, expense, docket-clearing pressure and procedural restrictions, encouraging discounted settlements and insulating existing rules from challenge. Delay commonly favors possessors, while repeat players can structure transactions to occupy that position. These are systemic mechanisms, not an assertion that every court or dispute exhibits identical bias.
qs: The presiding official acts as umpire, while the development of the case, collection of evidence and presentation of proof are left to the initiative and resources of the parties.
Thus, overload increases the cost and risk of adjudicating and shields existing rules from challenge, diminishing opportunities for rule-change.
overload tends to protect the possessor-the party who has the money or goods-against the claimant.

kp.k: Court cases reveal only part of dispute processing
kp.d: Galanter places adjudication within a broader landscape of litigation, court-oriented settlements, private remedies, exit and inaction. He distinguishes settlement systems dependent on official rules and sanctions from relatively independent private systems, while emphasizing that the boundary is a continuum. Litigation rates therefore cannot simply be read as measures of rights consciousness: costs, available alternatives, practical objectives and relationships influence whether people invoke courts.
qs: Our distinction between "appended" and "private" remedy systems should not be taken as a sharp dichotomy
The uneven and irregular layers are distinct although they merge imperceptibly into one another.
Public appetite for symbolic gratifica- tion by the promulgation of rules does not imply a corre- sponding private appetite for official vindication in terms of rules in particular cases.

kp.k: Continuing relationships can support private dispute resolution
kp.d: Galanter hypothesizes that enduring, inclusive relationships support informal sanctions and shared norms, making private resolution more likely. Litigation often occurs between strangers or after relationships break down. Important exceptions qualify this account: conflicts over fundamental values, government or monopoly relationships that limit exit, and repeat players lacking recurring dealings with each other may still generate litigation. Duration alone is insufficient; parties need opportunities to withhold cooperation or adjust the relationship.
qs: Units with mutually beneficial relations do not adjust their differences in courts.
Where RPs are contending about value differ- ences (who is right) rather than interest conflicts (who gets what) there is less tendency to settle
It is not temporal duration per se that pro- vides the possibility of control, but the serial or incremental charac- ter of the relationship

kp.k: Substantive rule reform alone has limited redistributive power
kp.d: Galanter argues that favorable rules can be absorbed without changing practical power relations when beneficiaries lack organization, representation or enforcement resources. Courts have particular limitations: they address party-framed cases, lack routine monitoring capacity and generally cannot finance new administrative machinery. Litigation can nevertheless provide protection, legitimacy, organizational opportunities and tactical advantages; the claim is limited effectiveness of rule change alone, not universal futility.
qs: Programs of equalizing reform which focus on rule-change can be readily ab- sorbed without any change in power relations.
Courts typically have no facilities for surveillance, monitoring, or securing systematic enforcement of their decrees.
Litigation then is unlikely to shape decisively the distribution of power in society.

kp.k: Capacity and service reforms address different structural barriers
kp.d: In explicitly hypothetical reforms, Galanter predicts that timely, individualized adjudication would reduce delay discounts and enable more rule challenges, benefiting many one-shotter claimants but also some repeat-player claimants. More active institutions could reduce dependence on private investigative and enforcement resources. Expanded legal services could improve outcomes but, without accompanying capacity changes, could also increase delay. Coordinated high-volume representation may instead use overload to pressure opponents into changing practices.
qs: Imagine an increase in institutional facilities for processing claims such that there is timely full-dress adjudication of every claim put forward-no queue, no delay, no stereotyping.
Enhanced capacity for securing compliance might be expected to reduce advantages flowing from differences in ability to invest in enforcement.
increase in litigation might mean even more delay

kp.k: Collective organization can convert one-shotters into repeat players
kp.d: Galanter identifies membership organizations, rights-management bodies, interest-group sponsors and information networks as ways to aggregate small claims, share unacceptable risks and sustain strategic representation. Organized groups can finance implementation as well as rule change. He presents class actions as potentially altering both sides' strategic positions without requiring claimants to finance conventional organization. Qualifications include collective-action barriers, unstable membership and the possibility that new organizations reproduce internal inequalities.
qs: An organized group is not only better able to secure favor- able rule changes, in courts and elsewhere, but is better able to see that good rules are implemented.
It can expend resources on surveillance, monitoring, threats, or litigation that would be uneconomic for an OS.
Such new units would in effect be RPs.

kp.k: Equalizing reform could increase both legalization and privatization
kp.d: Considering his reforms together, Galanter predicts a dual movement rather than uniformly more litigation. Reduced cost and information barriers would draw some disputes toward official remedies and bring court-oriented settlements closer to adjudicated outcomes. Organization of both sides could simultaneously support private bargaining and dispute systems. He expects more legalization for episodic relationships and more private ordering for continuing relationships, subject to organizational, value-conflict and monopoly exceptions.
qs: We would expect more use of the official system.
Relationships among strangers (casual, episodic, non-recurrent) would be legalized
Thus, delegaliz- ation would entail a kind of pluralism and decentralization.

kp.k: Implementation gaps accommodate local norms and unequal power
kp.d: Galanter interprets legal-system inefficiency as more than administrative failure. Cost barriers, ambiguity and overload permit field-level officials and constituencies to apply local priorities while authoritative law maintains universalistic commitments. This dualism accommodates social diversity and private power alongside formal unity and equality. Consequently, effective reform could expose relationships to authoritative rules previously avoided, generating pressure for explicit recognition of local values or decentralization.
qs: these field level legal communities produce regulatory outcomes which could not be predicted by examination of the authoritative "higher law."
It permits unification and universalism at the symbolic level and diversity and particularism at the operating level.

kp.k: Lawyers' reform contribution requires organization beyond courtroom advocacy
kp.d: Galanter recommends combining litigation and lobbying with interest organization, service provision and institutional innovation. He prioritizes reforms that improve parties' strategic capacities, including class actions, attorney-fee awards and provisional remedies. Lawyers are more likely to support redistribution when professional organization permits enduring client alliances, work beyond courts and a broad conception of legitimate professional tasks. He notes a paradox: professional flexibility that strengthens powerful recurrent clients can also enable lawyers to serve organized disadvantaged groups.
qs: It suggests that litigating and lobbying have to be complemented by interest organizing, provisions of services and invention of new forms of institutional facilities.
If rules are the most abundant resource for reformers, parties cap- able of pursuing long-range strategies are the rarest.
The question then is whether the organization of the profession permits lawyers to develop and employ skills at these other levels.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Galanter makes no claims about AI. His 1974 essay offers a theory of structural advantage in litigation and the limits of redistributive legal reform.
pts.d: In the source's own domain, Galanter argues that well-resourced repeat players can accumulate expertise, spread risk across cases, shape transactions and pursue favorable rules and implementation over time. He predicts that selective settlement and litigation can skew precedent toward repeat players. Legal representation and specialist lawyers can reduce some disadvantages of one-shot clients without eliminating repeat players' strategic advantages. Institutional passivity, overload, and complex rules reinforce these disparities. Substantive rule changes alone therefore have limited redistributive potential; organizing disadvantaged parties, improving services and institutional capacity, and combining these interventions offer stronger possibilities. These are Galanter's synthesis and conjectures, rather than claims about technological change.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence basis is an explicitly tentative synthesis of existing empirical studies, case accounts, professional observations and theoretical arguments, not a new causal test.
pts.d: Galanter supports his framework with studies of insurance settlements, creditor use of courts, manufacturer-dealer litigation, legal representation, enforcement of judgments and implementation of reforms. He reports Wanner's sample of 7,900 civil cases in three cities as consistent with organizational plaintiffs' advantages, rather than as proof of the entire repeat-player theory. He draws on Macaulay's account of automobile manufacturers' selective litigation to illustrate rule-shaping, Ross's research to discuss representation and settlement, and research on Detroit landlord-tenant proceedings to illustrate weak implementation of new tenant defenses. These underlying findings remain attributed to their cited researchers; Galanter supplies the broader structural interpretation. There are no AI benchmarks or AI-related evidence.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern an American-like legal system as analyzed in 1974, with advantages accumulating over repeated dealings; reform predictions are conditional thought experiments, not dated forecasts.
pts.d: The framework assumes unequal resources, complex procedures, specialized intermediaries, precedent effects, insufficient adjudicative capacity and incomplete implementation of authoritative rules. Repeat-player advantages depend on resources and the ability to pursue long-run interests, not repetition alone. Galanter treats one-shotters and repeat players as endpoints of a continuum and does not equate them categorically with poor and wealthy parties. His institutional-capacity scenario assumes timely adjudication of every claim; his legal-services scenario remains constrained by delay and risk unless other conditions change. Organization can facilitate private dispute settlement where parties expect continued mutually beneficial dealings, but value conflicts, monopolistic relationships and nonrecurring encounters qualify that prediction. He also qualifies the effects of litigation strategy on rule development and acknowledges variation in court activity and professional organization.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The analysis distinguishes organizational litigants, individual claimants and defendants, their lawyers, courts and reform organizations.
pts.d: Insurers, creditors, manufacturers, prosecutors and other adequately resourced repeat players gain from continuity, specialist services, risk spreading and long-run strategies. Injury victims, tenants, consumers, welfare recipients and other one-shot parties may face unaffordable enforcement costs, urgent stakes and weak implementation even after favorable decisions. Galanter argues that lawyers serving repeat players can provide more continuous and preventive assistance, whereas lawyers serving transient individual clients face recruitment barriers, processing incentives and competing institutional relationships. Unions, public-interest organizations, claims aggregators and coordinated legal-services programs may improve disadvantaged parties' strategic position. Such organization is not uniformly feasible and may recreate internal inequalities. Courts and enforcement agencies affect distribution through their procedures, capacity and allocation priorities.
